title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this card.
Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery.

Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.

status_note: The undated source survey explicitly asks for randomized polynomial-time factoring, and Harvey–Hittmeir Section 1.1 in the 5 June 2026 revision confirms the absence of a known polynomial-time factoring algorithm even with probabilistic methods. Bounded later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The cited heuristic estimate and quantum result are not certified as solutions in this classical model, and new proof claims were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

sentences: Integer factorization recovers the ordered primes and positive multiplicities whose product is a given positive integer.
The question asks for one classical randomized algorithm taking polynomial time in the number of input bits on every random sequence.
Its full factor list must be correct with probability at least two thirds separately on every positive input.
Efficient primality testing and verification do not resolve the task of finding the factors.
Known quantum algorithms, heuristic sieve estimates and improved deterministic subroutines each leave a different gap to this target.
